risks.note: The MD&A states that dependence on imported semiconductors and rare earth elements could constrain growth for the Indian auto component industry. For JBM Auto, whose components and EV aggregates carry rising electronic and magnet content (VCUs, BMS, telematics, ADAS, e-axles), a supply interruption or price spike in these inputs directly threatens production continuity and margin.
risks.risk: Dependence on imported semiconductors and rare earth elements

risks.note: Average battery prices fell 8% in CY 2025 but at the start of 2026 lithium prices were more than double their prior-year level, and the MD&A warns that sustained lithium and cobalt increases could raise the cost of lithium-ion batteries. Batteries are the single largest input in the e-bus and EV Aggregates verticals, so this is the dominant swing factor on e-mobility margins.
risks.risk: Battery raw-material and lithium price volatility

risks.note: The MD&A records that more than 90% of Indian electric bus sales are linked to State Transport Undertakings and that government procurement programmes have been the main growth catalyst, with the pipeline resting on FAME II, PM E-DRIVE, PM e-Bus Sewa and Purvodaya. Order visibility is therefore hostage to policy continuity, budget allocation and the pace of tendering; the MD&A notes PM E-DRIVE second-phase tendering is still underway and deployment begins only after concession agreements are signed between STUs and operators.
risks.risk: Concentration of e-bus demand in government procurement programmes

risks.note: The BRSR openness-of-business disclosure shows related parties accounted for 34.83% of purchases and 31.46% of sales in FY 2025-26 (up from 16% and 26%), 100% of loans and advances, and 94.09% of investments. That degree of intra-group dependence is a structural governance and transfer-pricing exposure and complicates assessment of arm's-length economics.
risks.risk: High share of related-party transactions in purchases, sales, loans and investments

risks.note: The BRSR records that the Company operates on a B2B model with products manufactured to specific OEM requirements, sells nothing through dealers or distributors (0% of sales), and locates several plants inside customer supplier and vendor parks (Ford, Renault-Nissan, Tata Motors, MVML, Toyota Kirloskar). Loss or programme cancellation at a single anchor OEM would strand dedicated capacity.
risks.risk: Customer concentration in a B2B, build-to-print OEM model

risks.note: BRSR Section A shows permanent employee turnover of 19.63% in FY 2025-26 and that 9,008 of 9,559 workers are other than permanent, i.e. contract labour. High attrition among permanent staff plus a predominantly contract shop-floor workforce is a structural risk to quality consistency and industrial relations, which the HR narrative addresses through contractor governance and engagement programmes.
risks.risk: Workforce attrition and reliance on non-permanent labour

risks.note: Following notification of the new labour codes on 21st November 2025 the Company had to restructure compensation elements and wage definitions with external consulting support, with cost implications on PF, ESI, gratuity and leave. The BRSR also discloses a GST penalty and interest levied by the Joint Commissioner ST, Chengalpattu on blocked input tax credit under Section 17(5) of the Tamil Nadu GST Act, stated by the Company to have no material impact.
risks.risk: Regulatory and compliance exposure, including the new labour codes and tax proceedings

risks.note: The MD&A notes that manufacturers globally are expanding production capacity and investing in next-generation technologies, that battery technologies and chemistries are advancing rapidly, and that sodium-ion could gain competitiveness against lithium. In a market where JBM has staked leadership on an integrated e-bus and battery platform, a chemistry or architecture shift would devalue existing product and process investment.
risks.risk: Competitive intensity and technology obsolescence in electric mobility

currentContext.expansion: JBM Auto's expansion in FY 2025-26 was described qualitatively rather than as a rupee capex programme. The Auto Components division reported ongoing investments in advanced manufacturing technologies and capacity expansion during the year, alongside enhanced manufacturing scale, automation and process integration across its facilities. The Tooling & Dies vertical expanded capacity to support rising demand from domestic and international OEM programmes, supported by enhanced design capability and greater adoption of automation and digital engineering tools, which reduced lead times and improved precision. On the e-mobility side, the Company states the group operates one of the largest electric bus manufacturing capacities globally at around 20,000 buses annually, and during the year strengthened its E-Mobility Platform through expanded deployment of electric buses across multiple cities, continued integration of charging and battery ecosystems, and new technology innovations such as the JBM E Verse. The largest named forward project is at the joint-venture level: subsequent to the close of the financial year, JBM Ecolife Mobility Private Limited secured a strategic investment of Rs 750 crore from Motilal Oswal Alternates directed at scaling e-bus deployment across India, with a planned rollout of approximately 2,000 energy-efficient e-buses. Structurally, the footprint per the Corporate Governance Report comprises fifteen JBM Auto plants across Haryana, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu and Gujarat - several of them located inside customer supplier or vendor parks - plus the JBM Electric Vehicles bus plant at Banchari (Hodal, Palwal, Haryana), the Indo Tooling plant at MHOW near Indore, the JBM Green Energy Systems plant at Bawal, and the two JBM Ogihara joint-venture plants at Bidadi (Karnataka) and Greater Noida. BRSR Section A reports 21 national plants/depots and 1 office (3 working depots, 18 plants, 1 office) with no international locations, and one new step-down foreign subsidiary, JBM Electric Vehicles Europe B.V., incorporated on 22nd July 2025. The AR does not state a rupee capex quantum: the Capital Commitments note supplied in this bundle carries only the label and the balance-sheet dates, with no figure attached.

PM E-DRIVE supports 14,028 e-buses across nine metropolitan cities with 13,800 allocated as of March 2026; PM e-Bus Sewa supports 10,000 e-buses in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities; Purvodaya funds 4,000 e-buses across eastern India.|The Bharat Urban Megabus Mission targets 100,000 e-buses by 2030 (versus an earlier 50,000) backed by an investment of Rs 1.75 lakh crore, aiming to raise public transport share to 60% of urban mobility.|India's e-bus market is moving from early adoption to large-scale deployment, with more than 10,000 electric buses already operating on Indian roads.|Procurement is increasingly structured through gross cost contract (GCC) and public-private partnership models, in which private operators procure, operate and maintain buses while transport authorities pay service-based fees - reducing the upfront burden on STUs and enabling larger volumes.|The Union Budget 2026-27 shifts EV policy from demand incentives to long-term ecosystem development, with PM E-DRIVE allocated Rs 1,500 crore through March 2028, enhanced PLI schemes, customs duty exemptions on critical capital goods and battery scrap, and Rare Earth Corridors to secure critical mineral supply.|The Indian auto component industry, on a US$ 80 Bn FY 2024-25 revenue base, has grown nearly 10% annually over the past five years and is projected to reach about US$ 200 Bn by CY 2030, with consolidation of global ICE supply chains creating a US$ 20-30 Bn export opportunity for Indian manufacturers.|Electrification is a structural demand driver for advanced components: technology-led shift is creating demand for EV-ready components, hot stamping and advanced thermal systems, with Indian EV sales expected to grow about 35% annually between CY 2024 and CY 2030.|The Indian battery market is projected to grow from US$ 12.68 Bn in CY 2025 to US$ 23.30 Bn by CY 2031 at a 10.71% CAGR, favouring EV Aggregates verticals focused on localised battery pack design, thermal management and assembly.|Battery cost is a margin lever with two-sided risk: average battery prices fell 8% in CY 2025, but lithium prices at the start of 2026 were more than double the prior-year level, and sustained lithium and cobalt increases could raise lithium-ion battery costs.|Commercial vehicle electrification is broadening the addressable base - electric CV penetration is still modest at 2.8% but monthly e-CV sales have more than doubled to 2,400 units on quick-commerce and last-mile delivery expansion.|JBM was India's top e-bus manufacturer in FY 2025-26, selling about 1,282 electric buses and capturing nearly 24% market share, backed by a strong order pipeline and continued expansion under national electrification programs.|Industry-level pipeline cited by management: awards for nearly 46,000 electric buses in India are scheduled for deployment over the next two to three years, providing strong visibility for continued market expansion.|The Auto Components division recorded sustained growth in orders during FY 2025-26, alongside expanded global OEM relationships.|The tooling division expanded capacity to support rising demand from both domestic and international OEM programmes.

risks.risk: Dependence on imported semiconductors and rare earth elements
risks.note: The MD&A states that dependence on imported semiconductors and rare earth elements could constrain growth for the Indian auto component industry. For JBM Auto, whose components and EV aggregates carry rising electronic and magnet content (VCUs, BMS, telematics, ADAS, e-axles), a supply interruption or price spike in these inputs directly threatens production continuity and margin.

risks.risk: Battery raw-material and lithium price volatility
risks.note: Average battery prices fell 8% in CY 2025 but at the start of 2026 lithium prices were more than double their prior-year level, and the MD&A warns that sustained lithium and cobalt increases could raise the cost of lithium-ion batteries. Batteries are the single largest input in the e-bus and EV Aggregates verticals, so this is the dominant swing factor on e-mobility margins.

risks.risk: Concentration of e-bus demand in government procurement programmes
risks.note: The MD&A records that more than 90% of Indian electric bus sales are linked to State Transport Undertakings and that government procurement programmes have been the main growth catalyst, with the pipeline resting on FAME II, PM E-DRIVE, PM e-Bus Sewa and Purvodaya. Order visibility is therefore hostage to policy continuity, budget allocation and the pace of tendering; the MD&A notes PM E-DRIVE second-phase tendering is still underway and deployment begins only after concession agreements are signed between STUs and operators.

risks.risk: High share of related-party transactions in purchases, sales, loans and investments
risks.note: The BRSR openness-of-business disclosure shows related parties accounted for 34.83% of purchases and 31.46% of sales in FY 2025-26 (up from 16% and 26%), 100% of loans and advances, and 94.09% of investments. That degree of intra-group dependence is a structural governance and transfer-pricing exposure and complicates assessment of arm's-length economics.

risks.risk: Customer concentration in a B2B, build-to-print OEM model
risks.note: The BRSR records that the Company operates on a B2B model with products manufactured to specific OEM requirements, sells nothing through dealers or distributors (0% of sales), and locates several plants inside customer supplier and vendor parks (Ford, Renault-Nissan, Tata Motors, MVML, Toyota Kirloskar). Loss or programme cancellation at a single anchor OEM would strand dedicated capacity.

risks.risk: Workforce attrition and reliance on non-permanent labour
risks.note: BRSR Section A shows permanent employee turnover of 19.63% in FY 2025-26 and that 9,008 of 9,559 workers are other than permanent, i.e. contract labour. High attrition among permanent staff plus a predominantly contract shop-floor workforce is a structural risk to quality consistency and industrial relations, which the HR narrative addresses through contractor governance and engagement programmes.

risks.risk: Regulatory and compliance exposure, including the new labour codes and tax proceedings
risks.note: Following notification of the new labour codes on 21st November 2025 the Company had to restructure compensation elements and wage definitions with external consulting support, with cost implications on PF, ESI, gratuity and leave. The BRSR also discloses a GST penalty and interest levied by the Joint Commissioner ST, Chengalpattu on blocked input tax credit under Section 17(5) of the Tamil Nadu GST Act, stated by the Company to have no material impact.

risks.risk: Competitive intensity and technology obsolescence in electric mobility
risks.note: The MD&A notes that manufacturers globally are expanding production capacity and investing in next-generation technologies, that battery technologies and chemistries are advancing rapidly, and that sodium-ion could gain competitiveness against lithium. In a market where JBM has staked leadership on an integrated e-bus and battery platform, a chemistry or architecture shift would devalue existing product and process investment.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: JBM Auto Limited, the flagship company of the JBM Group, is an integrated mobility solutions provider spanning advanced automotive components and next-generation electric mobility, and in FY 2025-26 emerged as India's top e-bus manufacturer with nearly 24% market share.

business_model.title: Business (RHP)
business_model.body: JBM Auto operates through five strategically aligned business verticals: Electric Buses, EV Aggregates, an E-Mobility Platform, Auto Components & Systems, and Tooling & Dies. themes.title: Auto components & EV-driveline localization
themes.need: Premiumization, content-per-vehicle rise and EV/hybrid transition pull a deep auto-ancillary chain - MOTHERSON/SONACOMS/BOSCHLTD/SCHAEFFLER/SKFINDIA/UNOMINDA-tier on driveline, bearings, wiring (MSUMI) and EV systems; OLAELEC/ATHERENERG/OLECTRA on EV OEMs (OLAELEC targeting cell-to-pack 10-15% cost edge); SUNDRMFAST/ENDURANCE/CRAFTSMAN/BHARATFORG on forgings/machining. Q1FY27 showed contracted pricing finally landing for Tier-2s: SSWL earned EBITDA/wheel of Rs 314 against Rs 262 YoY, which management attributed mostly to two years of OEM input-price increases finally landing (1-5%, more pending) rather than mix, with all plants above 95% utilisation and knuckles at 100%; KROSS delivered a 12.23% EBITDA margin (+63bps) BEFORE two retrospective pass-throughs land (steel settled ~15 July, the CV conversion-cost settlement still pending), making Q1 a floor rather than a peak.
themes.driver: GST 2.0 demand pull; retrospective OEM price pass-throughs still to land (KROSS CV conversion cost); EV cell/Gigafactory ramps (OLAELEC 6GWh by June); export + new-platform content wins.
